evidence.title: Herdr: Install; One Rust binary
evidence.finding: Herdr TUI runs as a Rust terminal program with a product CLI on macOS, Linux and Windows; it is not an Electron desktop client.

evidence.title: Herdr: Questions: How is it different; Which systems
evidence.locator: Questions: How is it different; Which systems
evidence.finding: The new Herdr native app supports Apple silicon macOS, Linux x86_64 and ARM64, and Windows x86_64. It is separate from TUI and does not share its running agents.

evidence.title: Herdr: Supported agents
evidence.finding: Herdr TUI runs existing agent CLIs in real terminal panes. Documented detections include Claude Code, Codex, Cursor Agent CLI, OpenCode, Pi, Grok CLI and Gemini CLI, with Gemini state detection labeled less tested. Other commands run as plain terminals.

evidence.title: Herdr: Install
evidence.finding: Install the Herdr binary or a package-manager build, start it where the repository lives and run existing agent commands. Saved SSH machines connect to their own server.

evidence.title: Herdr: Choose an integration layer; What you can control
evidence.locator: Choose an integration layer; What you can control
evidence.finding: Herdr provides CLI wrappers and a local socket API for workspaces, tabs, panes, agent prompts, waits, state events and integration management. The binary emits its matching JSON schema.

evidence.title: Herdr: Plugins
evidence.finding: Plugins extend Herdr terminal panes and workflows, with a marketplace and CLI/API management. This does not establish a built-in MCP client.

evidence.title: Herdr: One Rust binary
evidence.finding: Herdr TUI is a Rust binary running in the user terminal rather than an Electron app. This implementation statement does not describe the newer native app.

evidence.title: Herdr: What you can control
evidence.finding: Scripts and agents create and name workspaces, tabs and panes. These are terminal sessions rather than evidence of persistent native issue objects.

evidence.title: Herdr: Snapshot restore
evidence.finding: Saved session shape retains workspaces, tabs, panes, current directories, layout, focus and supported native agent session references. Agent reasoning memory remains harness-owned.

evidence.title: Herdr: Agents; State rollups
evidence.finding: Multiple agent terminals run concurrently; working, blocked, done and idle states roll up into tabs and workspaces. Observed concurrency and quotas remain untested.

evidence.title: Herdr: Raw methods
evidence.finding: Agents and scripts can start, prompt and wait on selected panes. agent.prompt refuses to send input when the resolved agent is already blocked. This is pane dispatch rather than task ownership enforcement.

evidence.title: Herdr: What you can control; Raw methods
evidence.locator: What you can control; Raw methods
evidence.finding: Herdr supplies agent start, read, prompt and event-driven wait operations to external agents and scripts. A wait pins the current pane occupant; Herdr does not thereby become a product-owned reasoning coordinator.

evidence.title: Herdr: Supported agents; Blocked state
evidence.finding: Known agents report or are detected as idle, working or blocked, with notifications when they finish or need input. Detection can fall back to idle for unfamiliar prompts; that is not permission to approve.

evidence.title: Herdr: State rollups
evidence.finding: The sidebar rolls a blocked pane up to its tab and workspace, and shows active work and done agents until viewed. No six-task fleet scenario was run.

evidence.title: Herdr: CLI examples
evidence.finding: Users can start one terminal task, split panes, prompt agents and wait on their state through the same CLI/socket control API.

evidence.title: Herdr: Connecting machines
evidence.finding: Local and saved SSH machines each own their server, sessions and processes. SSH interruptions leave remote work running; clients reconnect independently. The user supplies and pays for the host.

evidence.title: Herdr: Raw methods: Worktree
evidence.finding: The TUI socket exposes worktree.list, worktree.create, worktree.open and worktree.remove with workspace provenance. Git worktrees separate checkouts; no hostile-code containment is claimed.

evidence.title: Herdr: What survives; Snapshot restore; Native agent session restore
evidence.locator: What survives; Snapshot restore; Native agent session restore
evidence.finding: Detach keeps original processes alive. Server restart loses processes but restores layout, and supported integrations can resume native conversations. Optional pane screen replay is off by default; experimental live handoff is best effort.

evidence.title: Herdr: Snapshot restore
evidence.finding: Restored panes return to saved directories or remain visibly errored if the directory or shell is unavailable. Snapshot restore does not recreate arbitrary services or test processes.

evidence.title: Herdr: Raw methods: agent.wait
evidence.finding: Agent waits have explicit until and timeout_ms controls; an atomic prompt-and-wait avoids the race between separate operations. These are wait limits, not provider token or spend controls.

evidence.title: Herdr: How status works; Blocked state; Detection manifests
evidence.locator: How status works; Blocked state; Detection manifests
evidence.finding: State derives from screen manifests or integration reports. herdr agent explain exposes matched rules, source/version and idle fallback reasons. A process failure/approval fixture has not been induced.

evidence.title: Herdr: Saved data; Updates
evidence.finding: Remote connection authentication stays with OpenSSH. Saved machine profiles contain labels, target and session, but not passwords or private keys. This does not establish organization roles or SSO.

evidence.title: Herdr: Pane screen history replay
evidence.finding: Optional pane history stores recent terminal output locally and may contain secrets. It is disabled by default and is not an immutable audit log.

changes.summary: Coordinator re-judged under the written rule that applies to every product: Herdr v0.9.5 ships an agent skill that lets an agent running in a Herdr pane start agents in other panes, prompt them, read their output and wait for their state changes. A product-supplied coordinator role and delegation tools count even though the agent itself is third-party, as for other products with this pattern.

before.answer: Herdr supplies agent start, read, prompt and event-driven wait operations to external agents and scripts. A wait pins the current pane occupant; Herdr does not thereby become a product-owned reasoning coordinator.

after.answer: Herdr ships an agent skill and CLI that let an agent in a Herdr pane start agents in other panes, prompt them, read their output and wait on their state. The coordinating agent is a third-party CLI using these product-supplied tools.
